blogs.title: Hawaii, Again: Ninth Circuit Leans on § 1182(f) to Sustain Refugee Entry Suspension Pending Appeal
blogs.description: This post examines the panel’s reliance on Trump v. Hawaii to conclude the government is likely to prevail on the legality of Executive Order 14163 suspending refugee entries. It unpacks how the court applied Nken’s stay factors, emphasized the non-searching posture toward presidential findings under § 1182(f), and what that means for the Refugee Act’s structured admissions regime. It also considers the doctrinal throughline from Hawaii: the breadth of presidential authority over entry, the narrowness of judicial review, and the implications for future attempts to halt or reshape refugee admissions via proclamation.

blogs.title: When ‘Authorized’ Becomes ‘Obligated’: The Ninth Circuit Reads § 1522 as Requiring Post‑Admission Refugee Services
blogs.description: Focusing on the core statutory fight, this post analyzes the majority’s conclusion that 8 U.S.C. § 1522 imposes mandatory duties to provide reception and placement services to refugees already admitted to the United States—despite the government’s funding pauses and contract terminations. It contrasts that reading with Judge Lee’s partial dissent treating § 1522 as permissive, explores the canons at play (titles vs. operative text; ‘shall’ vs. ‘authorized’; ‘to the extent of available appropriations’), and explains how congressional appropriations and specific subsections using ‘shall’ (including for unaccompanied minors and early support projects) shape the court’s interim command to reinstate cooperative agreements.

blogs.title: An Unusual Stay: Appellate Court Stays Most Relief but Orders Reinstatement of Refugee Contracts
blogs.description: This post dissects the panel’s remedial posture: vacating earlier stays, largely staying the district court’s injunctions, yet directing the government to reinstate cooperative agreements necessary to deliver § 1522 services. It explores how Nken’s framework can justify affirmative, status‑preserving relief during an appeal, the court’s concern about the government’s inability to identify replacement providers, and the line the panel draws between presidential entry powers and agencies’ statutory obligations to those already admitted. It also flags what this means for appellate management of interim remedies and agency contracting during fast‑moving national policy shifts.

blogs.title: APA as Backstop: Agency Defunding Falters Even as the President’s Entry Bar Stands
blogs.description: This post explains how the panel bifurcates review of presidential action and agency implementation: while the President’s § 1182(f) entry suspension survives under Hawaii’s deferential lens, at least one APA challenge to agency defunding and contract terminations likely succeeds. It examines why the State Department’s termination of cooperative agreements and the government’s halting progress toward replacements expose the agencies to ‘contrary to law’ or arbitrary‑and‑capricious risk where Congress has funded refugee services and § 1522 sets obligations. The takeaway for administrative lawyers: EO‑driven policy shifts do not insulate agency funding and procurement choices from APA review when statutory duties to current beneficiaries remain.
